'Counterless' means a checkout-free, staffless store. 'Aegis' is a name, so keep it. UI strings: 'Scroll to experience' is a playful invitation (the pun on experience is optional to preserve), 'Let's talk' is a friendly button, and 'Feel free to reach out,' is a gentle lead-in to the email field. 'Made it this far?' is a cheeky, warm remark to a reader who scrolled to the bottom. 'Laiba's stalling. Click to skip' is a humorous loading message; keep the name Laiba and the joke tone (someone is slow, so the user can skip). Section headers (Industry, Academic, Creative, projects, explorations) pair across lines as one phrase ('Industry projects', 'Academic projects', 'Creative explorations'), so use matching wording. Almost every block is duplicated in the source (a heading or timeline repeated for animation); translate each repeat identically. Several headlines are split across segments and styled lines, so keep each fragment short and make them read together: 'A curious mind, / with a habit of making things.', 'Every chapter shaped, / how I see the world.', 'Design is how, / I make sense of complexity.', 'Some feelings, / find their way into words.', 'A little flavour, / goes a long way to the heart.' (adapt the idiom 'goes a long way' and 'the way to the heart is through...' naturally, don't translate literally), 'Four little paws, / a whole lot of personality.', 'Good things start / with' (continues into a call to action after the page ends). Segments marked ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧⟦2⟧ are inline-styled spans; keep the markers in place and let word order flex around them, keeping the emphasised phrase (e.g. 'making things', 'Lalitya Krishnan') inside its marker. Timeline rows use 'dates · place' or 'role/degree · institution': keep the · separator and the order; translate month names and 'Present' into the target language's usual forms and keep the numerals and ranges as they are (hyphen or en dash). Section eyebrows (A LITTLE ABOUT ME, MY JOURNEY, THE WAY I SEE THINGS, BETWEEN THE LINES, THE KITCHEN DIARIES, LIFE WITH LAIBA, AND THE STORY CONTINUES...) are all caps labels: keep them short and label-like. The three principles (Think in systems / Embrace complexity / Design with intention) recur as a framework, so render each term the same way throughout. Keep the quiet, parallel, aphoristic rhythm (triplets like 'community, discipline, and growing together'; 'Work shaped by logic. Life softened by words, warmth and wonder.') and preserve the contrast of logic against warmth. Keep a light humour in the Laiba lines ('occasionally supervising my design work'). 'Open Lipsa' is a button linking to his poetry platform: keep the name Lipsa and translate only 'Open'; 'View Resume' is a standard button. The Hindi poems 'धूप छाँव' and 'पठार' are the author's original verse and are already in the source language: do not paraphrase them. For Hindi, copy them verbatim and keep the line breaks. For other languages, either leave them verbatim with the title or give a faithful verse translation that keeps the line breaks, the rhyme where possible and the imagery (shimmering light and shade, swaying branches, mirage-like grass; a plateau that deflects sun and water yet breaks inside in silence), with the original beside it if the layout allows. The poem 'पठार' is in the first person (masculine: 'धरता हूँ', 'टूटता हूँ'). Keep the narrative factual: dates, institutions, and 'six years' of experience must stay exact. 'Persian kitten' is a cat breed. 'Hostel' means a residential boarding dormitory (Navodaya is a residential school), so do not render it as 'hotel'. 'Moulds' means manufacturing tooling, not fungus. Use a warm, sincere but not sentimental voice; avoid corporate stiffness.","dominantLanguage":"en"}

Where the sentence names the poems in Devanagari ('पठार, माया, बारिशें, and धूप छाँव'), keep the names as they are. 2) Many segments appear twice because of duplicated layout (desktop/mobile or animated headings). Split headings ('Why light and / colour matter', 'How we / approached it', 'What was / produced', 'What this project / taught me') are single phrases broken for layout, so translate them so each half still reads naturally on its own line. 3) The tone is humane and thoughtful. Keep 'we' for team work and 'I' for the author's own choices. The author is male, so use masculine first-person forms wherever the language marks gender (e.g. 'I chose language', 'gave me permission'). 4) Protect the imagery: the rainbow against storm clouds, the translucent glow of a butterfly wing, 'the eyes in the head on the body resting on the ground' (an embodied-perception quote, so keep its cumulative rhythm and do not simplify). 'Light and colour are not decorative, they are communicative' relies on the contrast, so preserve it. The aphorism 'Before structures defined space, light and colour established boundaries' should read as a poised, quotable line. 5) 'Colour' and 'Color' are used inconsistently in the source (the title says Color, the body says colour). Use one term consistently in the target language. 6) Emotion words (Lust, Envy, Serenity, Purity, Curious) are survey category labels. Choose precise emotion terms, not near-synonyms, and keep each one distinct. 'Lust' should stay frank but not vulgar. The card pairing Lavender with 'Passion' and 'romance · yearning · sensitivity' should keep the mid-dot separators. Keep the hex code and numbers as written, e.g. '50+ participants' and '2020'. 7) UI and microcopy ('Back to work', 'Let's talk', 'Thank you for the scroll.', 'Made it this far?', 'Good things start with a hello.', 'Feel free to reach out', 'Designed with', 'Made with') are friendly and witty. Adapt idiomatically rather than literally, keep them short, and keep 'Made with / Designed with' as an open-ended lead-in to an icon or heart that follows. Nav labels (Introduction, Process, Deliverables, Reflection) must match the section headings exactly. Keep '01'-'04' numerals. 8) Keep the copyright line and 'By Lalitya Krishnan' formal and short; transliterate the name in non-Latin scripts.","dominantLanguage":"en"}

communities","treatment":"translate","rendering":""}],"translationNotes":"The author is male: use masculine first-person forms wherever he speaks as I (e.g. 'I started with', 'I questioned', 'I selected') in gendered languages; 'we' in 'How can we...' is the generic design-question we, not personal. Much of the page is duplicated (responsive/animated copies and stacked headings); translate identical strings identically. Headings are split across segments with ⟦n⟧ markers (e.g. 'The hidden cost' / 'of convenience'; 'Using plastic,' / 'more responsibly'; 'Questioning' / 'the initial brief'): keep the marker order and make each fragment read naturally; reorder words only if the grammar demands it, and keep the markers. The short lines 'What if, instead of simply eliminating single-use plastics, / we explored new materials... / unlocks potential...' form one sentence broken over three lines (the source has a grammar slip, 'unlocks'); translate it as a single flowing sentence across the three lines with correct grammar. The opening imagery (a toy chest that holds stories, not plastic waste; a fleeting moment of joy before landfill) is the emotional hook: keep it vivid and concrete, and do not turn it into dry report language. 'Woven themselves into daily life', 'trail of destruction', 'loom large' and 'confront head-on' are figurative: adapt them to natural equivalents rather than going word for word. Keep 'web of interconnected challenges' as a web/network image if it works in the language. Section labels (Introduction, Context, Problem, Brief, Process, Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver) appear as nav, numbered tabs and headings: use one consistent rendering for each. Keep numerals 01–09 and 1–7 as they are. Keep acronyms (NID, SDGs) as written, with a translated expansion for the UN Sustainable Development Goals. The Indian context matters (Indian initiatives, rural livelihoods, agricultural residues): keep India-specific facts and the name 'Biomanufacturing Initiative' faithful, and translate the Indian government name as an official-sounding but plain term. Mind British spelling and mixed 'utilising/utilization'; this has no effect on meaning. The tone is constructive, not alarmist: avoid heightening the environmental language. Short UI-like items (tabs, buttons, bullet list of scope) should be concise and parallel in form (verb-led: Reduce..., Raise..., Create..., Build...). The 'Revised problem statement' is a long defined question: keep its full logic and all listed qualities (inclusive, practical, economically viable, sustainable across lifecycle, positive environmental, social and economic impacts) intact. 'Patra' is the product name and also an everyday word (leaf/plate) in several Indian languages, so keep it as written in Latin script (or transliterate only if native usage is natural) and never translate its meaning.","dominantLanguage":"en"}

electronics', '5D design / process', 'What this project / taught me', 'Identifying & understanding / problem area'): each line is part of one phrase, so render them so they still read naturally when stacked, even if word order shifts. 3) Section names (Introduction, Discover, Describe, Determine, Develop, Deliver, Process) are both nav labels and stage names of the 5D framework: use one consistent term for each everywhere, and keep the numbered nav (01–04) as is. The five stage names are a defined framework, so use verbs/nouns that match across the body sentence and the headings. 4) Keep all data literal: 50 million tonnes, 20%, 120 million tonnes, 2050, 17 SDGs, SDG numbers 3, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, '2022', and the '© 2026' line. Use the local convention for digits and number grouping, and the metric 'tonne' (not 'ton'). 5) 'A crisis hiding in plain sight' and 'disappears into an informal sector' are figurative: keep the idea of something visible yet ignored, and adapt rather than copy the idiom. 'Systemic reboot' is a metaphor meaning a fundamental overhaul; keep a tech-flavoured image if natural, otherwise convey 'fundamental reset'. 'Navigable complexity' and 'easy to get lost in' extend a journey metaphor; keep it. 6) 'Growing paradox of electronics' means technology both enables development and generates harmful waste; keep the tension. 7) The item lists under 'What are E-Products?' (Telephone, Facsimile & telex, Cellular phones, Fluorescent lamps etc.) are taxonomy entries: translate as plain nouns with consistent terms, keep the slightly clipped list style, and keep 'Equipments' as a plural category noun. 'Printing included cartridges' means printers including cartridges: translate the intended meaning. The source has minor typos and non-idiomatic phrases ('Economical impact' means economic impact; 'Understanding area'): translate the intended meaning, not the error. 8) The Reflection is the most personal passage: first person, male author, so use masculine forms where the language marks gender. Keep a thoughtful, slightly literary rhythm; 'ambiguity, interiority, and emotion' should stay as three distinct abstract nouns; 'gave me permission to be a designer and a poet at the same time' should sound sincere, not corporate. 9) The two lines 'Before structures defined space, / light and colour established boundaries.' are a poem fragment: preserve the line break, the lyrical cadence and the contrast between structures/space and light/colour, and do not turn it into prose. 10) The footer is playful and informal: 'Thank you for the scroll', 'Made it this far?', 'Good things start with a hello.' (the 'a hello' fragment is split from 'Good things start with', so make it work in sequence), 'Let's talk', 'Feel free to reach out,' and 'Designed with' (a heart or emoji icon probably follows, so keep it open-ended). Aim for a friendly, casual tone appropriate to the language, not stiff formality. 11) Keep UI strings short and idiomatic for buttons and labels ('Back to work' means return to the portfolio's project list, 'Email address', 'Let's talk'). 12) Credit lines ('Guided by Mr. Balaji Rengarajan', 'NID Bengaluru') keep the honorific and use the standard local form; transliterate names. The lone '·' bullets are decorative separators, so leave them untouched.","dominantLanguage":"en"}
